characterList.description: A middle-aged woman with short gray hair. She is the Head of the Department of Digital Resources at the Royal Armory, Skokloster Castle, and the Hallwyl Museum.
characterList.name: Karin Nilsson

content_metadata.description: This video explores the digitization project undertaken by the Royal Armory, Skokloster Castle, and the Hallwyl Museum, aiming to make their vast collections accessible to a global audience. It highlights the project's goals, the technology involved, and the impact on cultural heritage preservation and accessibility.

qAndA.answer: The museum aims to digitize the entire collection within 10 years.
qAndA.question: What is the timeframe for digitizing the entire collection?

qAndA.answer: High-quality images are essential to ensure the digital collection is usable for research, education, 3D printing, and other purposes.
qAndA.question: Why is the museum producing images of the highest quality possible?

qAndA.answer: The restoration of 'The Librarian' demonstrates the capability of digital technology to uncover hidden details and layers of history within artworks, making the digital object 'more real than reality.'
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the 'The Librarian' painting in the video?

qAndA.answer: The museum utilizes open licensing, making images and data freely available on its website, Google Arts & Culture, Europeana, and Wikimedia Commons.
qAndA.question: How does the museum ensure accessibility to its digital collection?

qAndA.answer: The project aims to preserve cultural heritage, make it accessible to a global audience, and foster new possibilities for engagement, research, and innovation.
qAndA.question: What is the ultimate goal of the museum's digitization project?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The Royal Armory, School Cluster Castle and the Halberd Museum constitute a museum agency
in Sweden. We tell the stories of the high society and the upper classes from the 17th century
to today. Two other museums are house museums with hundreds of rooms and the collection
within the museum. We have great collections of fine art, rare books, dresses, weapons,
you learn armories. My name is Karin Nilsson and I'm head of the department of digital
resources. We do have a lot of visitors to the museums but we also know that most people
in the world will never make it to the museums in Stockholm. So how can we reach the world
with all the stories we have in the collection? Our goal is to digitize the entire collection
quickly within 10 years with a very small funding. It means that we photograph as many objects
as once as we can, like a hundred rifles in one day. But at the same time we produce
images of the highest quality we're able to because otherwise no one will use it.
You make everything accessible online as soon as possible on our website, on Google
Art, in digital exhibitions on Europeana. If you like to use some of the objects yourself
you may 3D print for example this shield that used to belong to a former Swedish king
in the 16th century. On this model you're able to see details you will never be able to
see in the space of the museum. The digital object can actually be more real than reality.
Everything we do we do for the benefit of society. All the data we have in our systems,
all of the images in the collection are licensed with open licenses and everyone can use them
free of charge. The result is increased possibilities for the use and reuse of our material. For
example for children preparing schoolwork, for innovators building applications, or for
researchers who can study objects closely through high resolution images. All of the images
are also available on big media commons in the highest quality possible. We do big exports
of data from the collection management system so the images can be not only accessible but
truly useful. Just in a few months over 3 million people use the images and thousands of
article on Wikipedia in a lot of different languages use images from our collection. We
want to keep our digital collection open like when we restore paintings and we show what
the painting really looked like beneath the surface. This is a preservation of a famous
painting called the Liberian Brayarschenboldo. It is located as the cluster castle. On these
pictures you can experience what the painting looked like before, during and after the preservation
and it is an example of a process you can only get this close to in a digital world. The
result is now displayed in a digital exhibition where people all over the world can be amazed
at the details. When digitization in the museums is well performed is more real than reality
itself. In the space of the physical museums small rings are barely visible, fragile books
and paintings can be browsed to displayed but we still have to make these collections
available to the public. In recent years we have made the digitization of the collections
more efficient but we have also improved the quality of digitization. We hope that people
around the world will benefit from our work.

youtube_description:
How we make our collections accessible at the Royal Armoury, Skokloster Castle and the Hallwyl Museum.

This Ignite talk was first presented at the Europeana Network Association AGM in Amsterdam, 3-4 Nov 2015 by Karin Nilsson, director at the department of Digital Resources.
